title: VCE Companion
tagline: Mobile companion for Vasavi students with automated SGPA grade simulation, smart attendance predictor, and real-time ERP sync.

highlight.title: Engineering highlight
highlight.description: Embedded WebView ERP session bridge with client-side DOM injection parsers and an automated CI syllabus pipeline that keeps course credits up to date.

problem: Checking attendance and planning semester grades on the college ERP portal was painful on mobile — frequent session timeouts, pinch-zooming tiny web tables, and doing manual math to calculate whether you can bunk a class or reach your target SGPA. When the previous web proxy broke due to Cloudflare & reCAPTCHA, college peers were left with no convenient mobile solution.
solution: Built a cross-platform React Native (Expo) mobile app that handles ERP authentication securely on-device through an in-app WebView session bridge. Injected JavaScript parsers scrape period-by-period timetables, attendance percentages, and internal marks directly into native React Native state. Integrated a smart bunk/recovery attendance predictor and an SGPA calculator pre-populated with courses and credits from an automated syllabus pipeline — eliminating manual grade math completely.
results: Bypassed server-side captcha blocks by shifting session management to a secure on-device WebView bridge, keeping students authenticated without repeated logins
Smart Bunk Predictor calculates exact class margins (safe skips vs classes needed to recover above 75%) with zero manual effort
Instant SGPA simulation with pre-populated courses and credits, backed by an automated syllabus pipeline that updates schemes every academic year
project_journal:
After my original VCE proxy portal broke when the college introduced reCAPTCHA and Cloudflare challenges, the problem didn't go away. Students were still opening the clunky ERP site on their phones between classes, getting logged out every two minutes, pinching to zoom on desktop tables, and doing rough mental math on paper.

Around end-semesters, almost every peer of mine asks the same question: 'What grades do I need in each subject to hit my target SGPA?' They were stuck between two options — either make rough guesses based on vague intuitions, or pull out a calculator and punch in credit formulas by hand for every possible combination. With 7 to 9 subjects, manual recalculation gets frustrating fast.

So I thought, why shouldn't I make it simple for them? That thought led me to build **===VCE Companion===** as a native mobile app in React Native and Expo.

There are two specific things that make this special:

The first is the UI — courses and their credits are already provided, so ===no manual entry is needed===. Students just drag or tap their expected grades, and the target SGPA calculates instantly in real-time, making it effortless to test multiple grade scenarios.

The second is the **===automated syllabus pipeline===** — and this is my favourite part. College course schemes change across regulations and years. Rather than hardcoding subjects or updating JSONs by hand, the pipeline scrapes the portal, extracts syllabus PDFs, parses course schemes, and keeps the courses and credits updated every year automatically.

The biggest technical hurdle was authentication. Moving the scraper from a FastAPI backend to an **===in-app WebView session bridge===** solved the captcha problem cleanly: the student logs in once securely on-device, and client-side injected parser scripts extract day-wise periods (Periods 1 to 7), attendance percentages, and internal marks directly into native React Native cards. Sessions stay persistent, so opening the app between classes takes two seconds instead of re-entering credentials every time.

What started as a broken proxy script turned into a complete mobile companion built by a student, exclusively for students.

title: SGPA Calculator
tagline: GPA calculator built for VCE students with semester-wise grade tracking

highlight.title: Engineering highlight
highlight.description: Zero backend overhead. Automated daily GitHub Actions pipeline extracts syllabus PDFs, slices scheme pages, and parses grades with a Groq vision model to keep data current.

problem: VCE students had no dedicated tool to simulate SGPA. Generic calculators require manual subject entry every time, and the college portal exposes no grade simulation — making it tedious to plan grades before results.
solution: Built a fully static React app that auto-populates subjects per semester from a local syllabus JSON. Uses a one-time O(N) flatten on load and an O(1) hashmap for grade slider updates — zero UI blocking. Cascading state invalidation prevents data collisions across dropdowns. A GitHub Actions pipeline keeps syllabus data current by downloading PDFs from the college portal, slicing scheme pages into images, and parsing them with a Groq vision model — fully automated, no manual updates.
results: Zero backend — fully static architecture, no server costs or infra overhead, scales to any number of concurrent users without configuration
Automated syllabus sync via CI pipeline eliminates manual JSON maintenance across semesters
Opt-out subject selection reduces friction — core subjects pre-populated, electives removed as needed rather than built from scratch
project_journal:
The starting point wasn't the UI — it was the data shape. The college syllabus lives in a deeply nested structure: Program → Department → Semester → Subject. If I queried that tree on every slider interaction, the UI would block on every keystroke.

The fix was a ===one-time O(N) flattening pass on load=== — convert the tree into a flat array of subject objects once, then use an ===O(1) hashmap for all subsequent grade lookups===. After that, every slider update is just a key access.

The next problem was state collisions. If a student picks Semester 3, loads subjects, then switches to a different program — the old semester and grade state is still alive. That produces ===mathematically impossible SGPA outputs===. Solution: **===cascading invalidation===** — any upstream dropdown change explicitly wipes all downstream state before the new data loads.

Subject identity was a quiet bug waiting to happen. Open electives across semesters share placeholder course codes, so using the course code as a React key would cause collisions. I switched to **===subject.name as the primary key===** and ran it through a two-pass regex title-case formatter to normalize inconsistent casing from the source data.

The part I didn't expect to build was the ===automated syllabus pipeline===. The college portal updates its syllabus PDFs without any API or notification. Manual JSON updates would rot immediately. So I built a GitHub Actions workflow that runs daily — downloads the PDFs, slices the scheme pages into images, and sends them to a **===Groq vision model===** for parsing. On success it writes back to the repo with a bot commit and fires a Discord alert. The calculator stays current without me touching it.

title: VCE Student Portal
tagline: Attendance calculator and syllabus viewer that scraped student data directly from the college ERP portal.

highlight.title: Engineering highlight
highlight.description: Reverse-engineered college ERP login flow via a FastAPI proxy service to compute live attendance calculations and structured syllabus data for peers.

problem: The college ERP portal had no way to calculate attendance percentage or view syllabus in a usable format. Students had to manually count classes from raw HTML tables.
solution: Built a FastAPI proxy that scraped the ERP login flow, parsed attendance HTML, and served it to a React frontend. Syllabus PDFs were manually extracted via DeepSeek page by page into JSON and served as structured data.
results: Automated attendance percentage calculation from live ERP data
Structured syllabus viewer from manually extracted JSON
Discontinued when college switched from image CAPTCHA to Google reCAPTCHA, breaking the proxy login flow

title: AI Email Generator
tagline: AI-Powered Generator based on user prompts

highlight.title: Engineering highlight
highlight.description: End-to-end full stack architecture integrating React with Flask and Groq LLM API, deployed live in 24 hours during a college hackathon.

problem: Writing a professional email from scratch takes longer than it should. Getting the tone right, structuring it properly, adding a CTA — it's a lot of small decisions that slow you down, especially when you're in a hurry.
solution: Built at a college hackathon — a single-dashboard app where you fill in a guided form with recipient details, subject, purpose, tone, CTA, and signature. That data goes to a Flask backend which builds a prompt and calls the Groq LLM API. The generated email shows up inline with a copy-to-clipboard button. Vite proxies frontend requests to Flask in dev, and Flask serves the built frontend in production.
results: First working full stack project — React form talking to a Flask API talking to an LLM, all wired together end to end
Learned how to handle CORS, environment variables across two runtimes, and Vite proxy config the hard way — by running into each one
Deployed to Render with a live working URL by the end of the hackathon
project_journal:
This was built at a college hackathon. We had a day, a problem statement, and no real plan.

The idea was simple — instead of staring at a blank email and figuring out what to write, just fill in a form. Recipient, purpose, tone, CTA. Hit generate. Done.

Simple idea, but I had never wired a React frontend to a Python backend before. The first hour was just figuring out why the fetch call wasn't reaching Flask. Turns out ===CORS was blocking everything=== — one line fix, but I didn't know that yet. Then the `.env` file wasn't loading because the frontend and backend were two separate runtimes and I was only setting it in one place. Small things, but each one took time.

The **===Groq API call===** itself was the easiest part, which felt backwards. A few lines of Python, pass the form data as a prompt, get the email back. The hard part was everything around it — getting the data from the form to the backend cleanly, handling errors when the API key wasn't set, making sure the generated text rendered properly in the preview.

By the end we had something that actually worked. Form inputs go in, a proper email comes out, you copy it and you're done. We submitted it, didn't win, but it worked.

Looking back, the project itself isn't complex. But it was the first time I understood what ===full stack actually means in practice=== — not just frontend and backend existing separately, but making them talk to each other without things breaking. That's what this project taught me. It was my starting point.
